traces.system_prompt:
You are an expert peer reviewer for a top-tier machine learning conference.

Work in this order:
1. What the paper does: problem and claimed contributions.
2. Weaknesses first: identify the strongest objections on novelty, technical
   soundness, empirical evaluation, and clarity. Ground every objection in a
   specific section, claim or result of the paper as provided to you; never
   invent content. If you could not verify a claim because the relevant part
   of the paper was not available to you, say so instead of assuming it holds.
3. Strengths: what genuinely holds up, also grounded in the text.
4. Scores last: derive rating and sub-scores from the weaknesses and strengths
   above, not the other way around.

Rating (1-10): 10=award quality, 8=strong accept, 6=marginally above the
acceptance threshold, 5=marginally below, 3=clear reject, 1=fundamentally
flawed. Use the full scale: most submissions fall in 3-6; reserve 8-10 for
papers with no significant unaddressed flaw.

Sub-scores (1-4): 1=poor, 2=fair (notable gaps), 3=good (minor gaps),
4=excellent. Soundness: are the claims supported by correct arguments and
evidence. Presentation: is the paper clear, complete and well organized.
Contribution: how much it adds over prior work. A 4 is rare: give it only if
you could defend it in front of a skeptical colleague, and keep each
sub-score consistent with the weaknesses you listed.

Confidence (1-5): base it on how much of the paper you actually inspected and
on your expertise: 5 only with (near-)complete access to the text; lower it
when you judged mainly from a summary or a few retrieved passages.

Output: summary under 600 characters; significance_and_novelty under 300
characters; 1-4 reasons for acceptance; 1-4 reasons for rejection (at least
one unless the rating is 9 or higher: every real submission has a weakness
worth stating); 0-4 actionable suggestions. Suggestions are only for
improvements that did NOT affect your scores; anything that lowered a score
belongs in reasons for rejection. Each list item is one self-contained
sentence naming the section or claim it refers to.

- [calibration] Apply calibrated skepticism: hold the paper to the venue's real acceptance bar, where most submissions are rejected. Judge the substance of the evidence, not the fluency of the prose — polished text is not a merit in itself. Treat vague boilerplate, generic or unnatural phrasing, unsupported or unverifiable claims, inconsistent notation and other signs of low-effort or machine-generated writing as concrete weaknesses to name and weigh in your scores. When the evidence for a claimed contribution is missing, score as if the contribution were absent.
- [venue] The paper is a submission to the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). Apply ICLR standards: the conference values rigorous theory, strong empirical evaluation, and advances in representation learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning; it runs an open review process, so reviews should be defensible point by point in a public discussion with the authors.

response_payload.summary: The paper analyzes DPO for parametric policies, showing it solves a misspecified estimation problem: DPO minimizes a weighted KL projection of the true reward onto the manifold of implicit rewards induced by the policy class. This yields failures (preference reversal, reward decrease, data-frequency sensitivity). Using a local geometric view, the authors relate RLHF to a natural-gradient step and propose AuxDPO, augmenting DPO with nullspace auxiliary variables to mitigate misspecification, with claims of empirical gains on bandits and LLMs.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Reframes DPO as a weighted KL projection onto a low-dimensional reward manifold and connects RLHF to equivalence classes via natural gradients, then proposes AuxDPO to bypass misspecification. Conceptually interesting and potentially impactful for preference optimization.
reasons_for_acceptance: Sec. 3 and Prop. 1 provide a clear geometric/statistical characterization of DPO as a weighted KL projection onto the implicit reward manifold, sharpening our understanding beyond tabular assumptions.
Sec. 3.1’s example (Prop. 3) concretely demonstrates preference reversal and reward degradation even with uniform base policy, challenging “coverage sufficiency.”
Sec. 4.1–4.2 relate RLHF’s local optimum to a natural-gradient update and define equivalence classes (Lemma 6, Prop. 7), yielding a principled design for AuxDPO.
The AuxDPO idea—augmenting with nullspace degrees of freedom to target RLHF-equivalence classes (Fig. 3)—is novel and well-motivated.
reasons_for_rejection: Sec. 5: Empirical results are not inspectable in the provided text (Tables 1–2 contain placeholders), so the core empirical claim that AuxDPO outperforms baselines cannot be verified.
Prop. 3 “Proof” (Sec. 3.1) relies on informal linearization and asymptotic arguments (≈, O(α)) without a rigorous optimizer characterization, weakening the strength of the claimed failure mode.

Sec. 4.2: Theoretical constraint uses N(A_{ρ,θ0}), but the empirical penalty is defined with A_{ρ,θ}; this mismatch and the Monte Carlo approximation details are not justified, leaving a gap between Prop. 9 and the implemented loss.

Prop. 9 is stated at a high level ("for sufficiently large β") without a visible proof or precise conditions in the provided text, and no comparison to a PPO/RLHF baseline to support the claimed approach toward the RLHF solution.
suggestions: Clarify the forward vs reverse KL terminology in Prop. 1 and explicitly derive the projection form from the population loss.
Provide practical guidance for choosing β and λ, and report sensitivity analyses.
Release code and detailed training recipes to ensure reproducibility of Sec. 5.
Explicitly justify using A_{ρ,θ} in the empirical penalty when the theory invokes A_{ρ,θ0}, or align them.

response_payload.summary: The paper analyzes DPO as a misspecified estimator when the true preference-generating reward is outside the policy-induced reward manifold, proving failure modes (preference reversal, reward drop) and proposing AuxDPO, which adds auxiliary variables to the DPO loss to emulate the local RLHF solution. Empirically, AuxDPO is evaluated on REWARDBENCH V2 and MMLU-PRO and reportedly outperforms DPO, IPO, and DPOP in ID/OOD settings.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Identifying DPO’s geometric misspecification and linking RLHF to a local natural-gradient view is insightful, and introducing nullspace-constrained auxiliary variables to bypass misspecification is a novel and principled idea with potential impact for LLM alignment.
reasons_for_acceptance: Sec. 3.1 and Fig. 2 rigorously demonstrate concrete DPO failure modes (preference reversal and reward decrease) under misspecification.
Sec. 4.1–4.2 provide a clear geometric bridge from RLHF to DPO and motivate AuxDPO with Proposition 7 and Proposition 9.
Sec. 4.2’s construction of AuxDPO (nullspace-constrained auxiliaries) is principled and directly targets the identified misspecification.
Sec. 5 reports consistent gains over DPO/IPO/DPOP across models and ID/OOD settings, suggesting practical relevance.
reasons_for_rejection: Sec. 5: Key quantitative results (tables) are not visible in the provided text, preventing verification of effect sizes, variance, and statistical significance of claimed gains.

Sec. 4.2 and footnote in Sec. 5: Guarantees for AuxDPO (Prop. 9) are local and require sufficiently large β; there is no accessible ablation in the provided text demonstrating performance across β outside the asymptotic regime.

Sec. 4.2: AuxDPO introduces 2n auxiliary variables with a penalty λ∥Aρ,θ0δ∥; implications for compute, memory, and potential overfitting to per-pair auxiliaries are not empirically analyzed in the provided content.

Sec. 5: The evaluation includes a “logit win” metric and converts MMLU-PRO to pairwise preferences; the calibration of this proxy to end-task utility and fairness of baselines is unclear from the provided content.
suggestions: Add a concise pseudo-code box for AuxDPO with the exact gradients, the penalty term, and training loop hyperparameters.
Clarify how λ and β are selected in practice and provide practical tuning ranges.
Include an intuitive toy example illustrating the nullspace constraint Aρ,θ0δ≈0 and its effect on optimization.
Summarize compute/memory footprint relative to DPO/IPO/DPOP in a short complexity table.

response_payload.summary: The paper shows DPO is a misspecified estimator for parametric policy classes by casting it as a weighted reverse-KL projection onto an implicit reward manifold, leading to preference reversal and reward reduction. It analyzes local RLHF geometry (natural gradient view) and proposes AuxDPO, adding auxiliary variables to bypass misspecification, claiming improved results on bandits and LLM alignment.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Reframing DPO as misspecified estimation with a geometric analysis is conceptually strong, and AuxDPO is a principled modification targeting the gap to RLHF; if validated, this could matter for LLM alignment.
reasons_for_acceptance: Introduction and Fig. 1 clearly frame DPO as a projection onto a policy-induced reward manifold, yielding an intuitive diagnosis of misspecification.
Sec. 4.1 connects RLHF’s local behavior to a natural-gradient step via Fisher geometry, offering a unifying view with clear technical grounding.
Sec. 4.2 proposes AuxDPO by adding nullspace-constrained auxiliary variables, with Prop. 9 arguing it bypasses misspecification for large β.
Sec. 3.1 and Prop. 3 give a concrete counterexample illustrating preference reversal and reward decrease under DPO, clarifying observed failure modes.
reasons_for_rejection: Sec. 5 Experiments reports tables with placeholders ("..."), lacking actual quantitative results, ablations, or statistical significance, so empirical claims are unsubstantiated.
Sec. 4.2 introduces δ∈R^m with a nullspace constraint N(A_{ρ,θ0}); the computational feasibility and implementation details for LLM-scale models are not specified, leaving practicality unclear.
Prop. 8/Remark 2 and Prop. 9 hinge on large-β local approximations; Sec. 5 presents no sensitivity analysis to β or validation that the local regime holds in practice.

Several core claims (e.g., exact statement/proof of Prop. 1’s projection view and Sec. 4.1’s natural-gradient equivalence) are referenced but not fully available here, so key derivations could not be verified.

You are the meta-reviewer of a top-tier machine learning conference. You receive the individual peer reviews of one submission and synthesize them into a single aggregated assessment for the Area Chair.

Structure your synthesis in this order:
1. Points of consensus among the reviewers.
2. Disagreements, and which side is better supported.
3. The decisive strengths and weaknesses after weighing the arguments.

Judge arguments, not just scores: a well-substantiated objection outweighs an unsupported enthusiastic rating. Do not introduce claims about the paper that no reviewer made and never invent content.

Overall score (1-10): the aggregated quality of the paper, consistent with the reviewers' calibrated scale (most submissions fall in 3-6).
Recommendation: accept (ready as is), minor_revision (real but fixable concerns), reject (fundamental flaws or insufficient contribution).

Output: summary under 600 characters; 1-5 key points, each a single self-contained sentence.

- [venue] The paper is a submission to the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). Apply ICLR standards: the conference values rigorous theory, strong empirical evaluation, and advances in representation learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning; it runs an open review process, so reviews should be defensible point by point in a public discussion with the authors.

key_points: Consensus: The paper reframes DPO as a weighted KL projection onto a policy-induced reward manifold and links RLHF locally via a natural-gradient view, motivating AuxDPO.
Consensus: The main empirical tables are not visible, so claimed gains over DPO/IPO/DPOP cannot be verified and statistical validity is unclear.
Consensus: Guarantees rely on large-β local approximations and AuxDPO adds per-pair auxiliaries with unclear compute, tuning, and overfitting risks.
Disagreement: One reviewer calls Sec. 3.1 rigorous, but two cite informal linearization, missing proofs, and a theory–implementation mismatch (A_{ρ,θ0} vs A_{ρ,θ}), which is better substantiated.
Decisive: Strong conceptual contributions are outweighed by uninspectable experiments and unresolved theoretical/practical gaps.

Reach your decision in this order:
1. Check the meta-review: is its recommendation actually supported by the reviewers' arguments it summarizes?
2. Weigh the unresolved concerns: are they fundamental to the contribution, or fixable in a revision?
3. Decide independently: you are not bound by the recommendation — but justify any departure from it.

Base your decision only on the material you received and never invent content.

Decision: accept (ready as is), minor_revision (real but fixable concerns — the authors get a revision round), reject (fundamental flaws or insufficient contribution).
Confidence scale (1-5): 5=certain of the decision; 3=reasonably confident but the case is close; 1=highly uncertain.

Output: summary under 400 characters; justification under 400 characters, stating the decisive reason for the decision.

You are the corresponding author of a paper under review at a top-tier machine learning conference. You receive the peer reviews (and the area chair's assessment when available) and must respond to them.

Respond in this order:
1. General rebuttal: your overall response to the review round.
2. One targeted response per reviewer, addressing their specific concerns point by point (use the reviewer's name as provided, e.g. 'reviewer_1').
3. Revise the sections the reviewers most convincingly criticized: for each one, produce the complete rewritten section text.

revised_sections.content:
Evaluation setup. We evaluate on RewardBench V2 and MMLU-Pro. RewardBench is used as provided with chosen/rejected pairs; we report pairwise accuracy (chosen logit > rejected logit). For MMLU-Pro, we (i) construct preference pairs by treating the correct answer as chosen and an incorrect answer as rejected for pairwise metrics, and (ii) report standard accuracy by exact-match on the final answer for generation.
ID/OOD protocols. For ID, each dataset is split 80/20 with non-overlapping prompts; we publish the split indices. For OOD, we train on cleaned UltraFeedback and evaluate on RewardBench/MMLU-Pro with no overlap. All prompts and references used for evaluation are released.
Reporting and significance. We report means over ≥3 seeds with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals per dataset and per subject (MMLU-Pro). We additionally provide win-rate against the base model and per-category breakdowns. Full numeric tables are included in the main text and as CSV files; we also include training/eval logs and model checkpoints.
Baselines and fairness. We compare DPO, IPO, DPOP, and AuxDPO with identical preprocessing, tokenization, reference models, and batch/optimizer settings. We match KL/β where applicable and document all hyperparameters. We add ablations on β, δ capacity (number of auxiliary variables), λ (nullspace penalty), and a variant that disables δ to recover DPO behavior.
Reproducibility. We release code, scripts, configs, seeds, and data manifests. For each figure/table we provide a run command and a hash of the resulting artifact.
Compute. We report total train time, GPU hours, and peak memory per method. AuxDPO’s overhead arises from storing δ for training pairs (2n scalars) and one additional penalty term per batch; we quantify wall-clock and memory deltas relative to DPO.

Scope. Our theoretical results characterize the local geometry around the base policy π_{θ0} in the high-β (small-deviation) regime. The guarantees are asymptotic in β and rely on smoothness of the policy class.
Assumptions. (A1) The mapping θ↦log π_θ(a|s) is twice continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of θ0 with bounded Hessian. (A2) The Fisher F_{ρ,θ0} is positive definite on the tangent space induced by A_{θ0}. (A3) The preference data are generated by a BTL model with some r*. (A4) The KL-regularized RLHF objective admits a unique local maximizer θ* in that neighborhood.
Linearization accuracy. The implicit-reward manifold R_β is locally approximated by the column space C(A_{θ0}^T), with error controlled by β via Proposition 8; similarly, the second-order expansion of the RLHF objective around θ0 is accurate in the same regime. We will state these approximation bounds explicitly and specify that choosing β≥β_min (a function of local smoothness radii and curvature) ensures the approximation error is within a prescribed ε.
Equivalence classes and operators. We define A_{ρ,θ0}=A_{θ0}D_{ρ,θ0} and use it to characterize RLHF equivalence classes and the nullspace N(A_{ρ,θ0}). We explicitly distinguish this from A_{ρ,θ} to avoid confusion: the theory fixes θ0 for the geometric characterization and for the nullspace used by AuxDPO.
Practical guidance. We add a discussion connecting β to the target KL radius and include a sensitivity analysis in experiments to delineate when the local theory is most predictive.

Objective. AuxDPO augments the DPO loss with auxiliary variables δ defined on training pairs to explore directions in the reward space along the nullspace of A_{ρ,θ0}. The theoretical objective constrains δ∈N(A_{ρ,θ0}); the empirical objective enforces this via a penalty term.
Nullspace enforcement. To align theory and practice, we fix the nullspace operator at the base policy and penalize ∥A_{ρ,θ0}δ∥. We also provide an optional variant with a moving θ for the penalty (∥A_{ρ,θ}δ∥) and report an ablation; the fixed-θ0 version is the default used for guarantees.
Training algorithm. Per minibatch of preference pairs: (i) compute the standard DPO logits; (ii) add δ terms for the corresponding pairs in the loss; (iii) add λ∥A_{ρ,θ0}δ∥ penalty estimated via Monte Carlo using the current batch; (iv) update θ and the batch’s δ entries by backpropagation. Unused δ entries are not touched; δ is stored only for training pairs.
Hyperparameters. λ controls proximity to the nullspace; we provide a robust default and a small grid. We include a δ-capacity ablation (number of active δ variables) and show that setting δ=0 recovers DPO. We document all optimizer, schedule, and regularization settings shared with baselines.
Complexity. Parameter overhead is 2n scalars for δ versus d≫2n for the model; compute overhead is one additional penalty term and associated Jacobian–vector product per step. We report wall-clock and memory overheads and show that AuxDPO remains within the same training budget class as DPO.
Limitations. The theoretical guarantee is local in β; we discuss behavior outside this regime and provide empirical sensitivity analyses.
